items.title: 33.5 Effect of Water Pollution on the Environment

source_refs.note: Topic 33.5 with Quick Check 33.5 (PDF 255-256); the biomagnification diagram is original. Quick Check answers were derived for the lesson and need review.

blocks.text: Pollutants can change the physical and chemical properties of water, making it hard for plants and animals to survive. Common environmental impacts are loss of biodiversity, destruction of habitats, disruption of food chains and decline in water quality.

items: Destruction of ecosystems and biodiversity: oil, heavy metals, pesticides, plastics and waste damage aquatic life. Polluted water has less oxygen (hypoxia), damages coral reefs and disrupts food chains, breeding cycles, food sources and migration, leading to population decline and even extinction of sensitive species; birds and animals that depend on water are affected too.
Nutrient overload (eutrophication): excess nitrogen and phosphorus from fertilisers and sewage cause rapid algal growth, which blocks sunlight and lowers oxygen, killing fish and other species.

Bioaccumulation and biomagnification: toxins such as mercury, lead and pesticides build up in organisms over time and become more concentrated as they move up the food chain; top predators, including humans, often receive the highest doses.

Soil degradation and damage to plant life: heavy metals, industrial waste and excess nutrients seep into soil, changing its structure and fertility and disrupting its microbes; plants watered with polluted water may show stunted growth, discoloured leaves, or die.

Methane from decaying organic matter: sewage, farm runoff or industrial waste boost the growth of algae and other organisms; when these die and decompose in oxygen-poor (anaerobic) conditions, methane, a potent greenhouse gas, is released, adding to climate change and global warming.

blocks.alt: Five boxes of increasing height joined by arrows: water, plankton, small fish, large fish, and top predators including humans. Red dots for a toxin such as mercury, lead or a pesticide become more numerous in each box from left to right.
blocks.caption: Bioaccumulation and biomagnification (original diagram for topic 33.5).
blocks.long_description: Each animal eats many of the organisms below it and stores the toxin instead of excreting it, so the concentration rises at every step of the food chain.

blocks.prompt: Methylmercury, [CH3Hg]+, is 'highly fat-soluble'. Contrast it with the inorganic Hg2+ ion and explain why the methyl group changes its solubility in the lipid bilayers of cells.
blocks.explanation: Hg2+ is a small, highly charged ion that is strongly hydrated, so it stays in water and does not cross non-polar membranes easily. In [CH3Hg]+ a non-polar methyl group is bonded to mercury and the overall charge is only 1+, so the species is far less polar and dissolves in the non-polar lipid bilayer, crossing membranes and the blood-brain barrier.

blocks.prompt: Predict the effect on biomagnification if [CH3Hg]+ were very water-soluble but had low fat solubility.
blocks.explanation: Biomagnification would be much smaller: a water-soluble substance is excreted more easily and is not stored in fatty tissue, so it would not build up at each step of the food chain.

blocks.prompt: How can water pollution contribute to global warming?
blocks.explanation: Sewage and nutrient runoff boost the growth of algae and other organisms; when they die and decompose in oxygen-poor (anaerobic) water, methane, a potent greenhouse gas, is released.

items: Effects: ecosystems and biodiversity, eutrophication, biomagnification, soil and plants, methane.
Top predators, including humans, receive the highest toxin doses.
